# Which resolver wrote this record

A record resolved on a GitHub runner carries a resolver identity with no
commit in it:

    "resolvedBy": { "basis": "bundle_digest", "digest": "d32543070474cc28" }

That is the SHA-256 of the one-file resolver the Action ran, truncated to
sixteen characters. GitHub downloads an action as a tarball rather than
cloning it, so the running code has no git history beside it to name a
commit from. This table is the missing half: look the digest up here and
it becomes a commit in a public repository, with a date and a size.

Every row is derived. Nothing in this file is typed by hand, and
`npm test` fails if it stops matching the repository's history.

## Reading a row

Take the digest off the record and run the lookup, which prints the row above and the commit it names:

```
cd ursa-major && npx tsx tools/make-bundle-digest-index.ts --lookup d32543070474cc28
```

Or read the bundle itself, byte for byte, out of the commit the row names:

```
git cat-file blob 4b3a790ecd47eaa76dc4fe646feaf2a3ff704a4c | sha256sum
```

## What "introduced by" means, exactly

The commit that holds this version of the bundle while none of its
parents do. It is the commit on the branch where the bundle was rebuilt,
not the merge that brought it to `main`, so the date is when the bundle
was built rather than when it shipped. A row names more than one commit
only if the same bytes were introduced twice, which a revert can do.

## The one rule for contributors

A commit cannot index its own bundle: the row names a commit hash that
does not exist until the commit is made. So rebuilding the bundle takes
two commits in the same pull request — `npm run bundle` and commit, then
`npm run provenance:bundles` and commit. Between them `npm test` fails
with the digest that has no row.
